description.en: Twelve centuries in a few minutes: from the legendary founding of Rome through the Republic, the Punic Wars and Caesar to the Empire and its fall in the West.

text.en: Roman tradition holds that Romulus founded the city on the Palatine Hill on 21 April 753 BC. Romans counted years 'from the founding of the City', and the small settlement grew into the centre of a vast empire.

According to tradition, the Romans expelled their last king, Tarquin the Proud, and created a republic led by two annually elected consuls. The Republic lasted nearly five centuries and inspired modern political thought.

At the start of the Second Punic War the Carthaginian general Hannibal led an army with war elephants from Spain across the Alps into Italy. He lost nearly half his men but went on to crush the Romans at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae.

After a three-year siege, Scipio Aemilianus took and razed Carthage, selling its survivors into slavery. Its land became the Roman province of Africa, leaving Rome the sole great power of the Mediterranean.

In 73 BC some seventy slaves led by the Thracian Spartacus broke out of a gladiator school in Capua. His army grew to tens of thousands and defeated Roman legions for two years, until Crassus crushed it in 71 BC; six thousand captives were crucified along the Appian Way.

In eight years Julius Caesar subdued Gaul, roughly modern France and Belgium; the decisive moment was the siege of Alesia in 52 BC, where Vercingetorix surrendered. The conquest gave Caesar wealth and a loyal army with which he soon seized power in Rome.

On the Ides of March, senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed the dictator Julius Caesar to death at a Senate meeting in the Curia of Pompey. Instead of saving the Republic, the murder unleashed new civil wars that brought Octavian to power.

The Senate granted Octavian the honorific name Augustus. Keeping republican forms while holding real power, he created the Principate; the year is conventionally taken as the start of the Roman Empire and the Pax Romana.

In July 64 a fire raged through Rome for six days and destroyed much of the city. According to Tacitus, Nero was away at Antium; on his return he opened the Campus Martius and his own gardens to the homeless.

title.en: Battle of Edessa: a Roman emperor taken captive

text.en: The Sasanian king Shapur I crushed a Roman army near Edessa and captured Emperor Valerian along with his staff. Valerian died in captivity in Persia.

Emperors Constantine and Licinius agreed at Mediolanum to grant freedom of worship and restore property seized from Christians. Persecution ended, and with Constantine's patronage Christianity rapidly became the religion of the empire.

On the death of Theodosius I, the last emperor to rule the whole empire, it was permanently split between his sons: Arcadius took the East and Honorius the West. The West fell 81 years later, while the East (Byzantium) endured another thousand years.

title.en: Sack of Rome by the Visigoths

text.en: The Visigoths under Alaric captured Rome and plundered it for three days — the first time in almost 800 years that the city fell to a foreign enemy. The shock was immense and moved Augustine to write The City of God.

title.en: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

text.en: The Germanic commander Odoacer deposed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople. The year is traditionally taken as the end of the Western Roman Empire and the line between antiquity and the Middle Ages.

source: Steps assembled from the event records included in this atlas.
